entry.title: Loon4Mac TCP Performance Test
entry.summary: Local TCP performance of Loon4Mac on an Apple M1 Max, with automated and manual test instructions.
entry.content:
Loon4Mac Build 1007 improves TCP forwarding performance. On an Apple M1 Max, a single upload stream reached 12.25 Gbps, a single download stream reached 13.97 Gbps, and four download streams reached a combined 20.61 Gbps.

Results​

Test environment​

ItemConfiguration
DeviceApple M1 Max with 32 GB of memory
SystemmacOS 27.2
LoonLoon4Mac Build 1007
Test toolApple iperf3-darwin 3.8.1
TUN MTU4000

Test traffic originated on the Mac and passed through Loon's TUN and TCP stack to a local iperf3 server. Each test used a 2-second warm-up and a 10-second measurement period and was run once.

TestTCP throughputPeak Loon NE RSS
Single-stream upload12.25 Gbps55.70 MiB
Single-stream download13.97 Gbps59.28 MiB
Four-stream upload (combined)10.67 Gbps60.55 MiB
Four-stream download (combined)20.61 Gbps90.23 MiB

Before testing, Loon NE used approximately 46.45 MiB of RSS while idle. The four-stream values are the combined throughput of four TCP connections. RSS is the memory used by the entire Loon network extension process, not by a single connection.

Test procedure​

Loon configuration​

Merge the following entries into the current configuration. Place the DOMAIN rule before FINAL:

[Host]
bench.loon.test = 127.0.0.1

[Rule]
DOMAIN,bench.loon.test,DIRECT

Save the configuration and connect Loon. Do not add bench.loon.test to real-ip or the system /etc/hosts file.

Automated test script​

Download the Loon4Mac TCP test script

Run it after downloading:

/bin/bash ~/Downloads/loon4mac-tcp-test.sh

The script tests single-stream upload, single-stream download, four-stream upload, and four-stream download in sequence, records Loon NE RSS, and saves the results in the current directory.

Manual testing​

Start the server in one Terminal window:

/usr/bin/arch -arm64 /usr/bin/iperf3-darwin -s -B 127.0.0.1 -p 5201

Run the following commands in another Terminal window:

# Single-stream upload
/usr/bin/arch -arm64 /usr/bin/iperf3-darwin -c bench.loon.test -4 -p 5201 -O 2 -t 10 -i 1

# Single-stream download
/usr/bin/arch -arm64 /usr/bin/iperf3-darwin -c bench.loon.test -4 -p 5201 -O 2 -t 10 -i 1 -R

# Four-stream upload
/usr/bin/arch -arm64 /usr/bin/iperf3-darwin -c bench.loon.test -4 -p 5201 -O 2 -t 10 -i 1 -P 4

# Four-stream download
/usr/bin/arch -arm64 /usr/bin/iperf3-darwin -c bench.loon.test -4 -p 5201 -O 2 -t 10 -i 1 -P 4 -R

For single-stream tests, use the final receiver result. For four-stream tests, use [SUM] receiver. The client must connect to bench.loon.test; traffic sent directly to 127.0.0.1 does not pass through Loon.

entry.title: Loon4Mac DHCP Guide
entry.summary: Learn the requirements, configuration, device policies, lease management, and precautions for Loon4Mac DHCP.
entry.content:
Loon4Mac DHCP (Build 1007+) automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, default gateways, and DNS settings when devices join the LAN. Loon4Mac can provide an independent DHCP service on a wired network and use global or per-device policies to decide whether each device uses the Loon gateway and whether Loon intercepts its UDP DNS traffic.

Before you begin​

DHCP affects new devices and devices renewing their leases across the LAN. Check the following before enabling it:

  1. Your Mac is connected through wired Ethernet. Loon DHCP does not provide service through a Wi-Fi interface.
  2. The Ethernet interface uses a static IPv4 address. The setup wizard checks the current configuration and can make the current address static.
  3. Other DHCP servers on the LAN are disabled. Home routers normally provide DHCP, so disable that service in the router's administration page first.
  4. Loon VPN is connected. DHCP runs inside Loon's network extension.
  5. Your Mac remains powered on and awake. Loon cannot respond to DHCP requests if the Mac sleeps, Ethernet disconnects, or the VPN stops.

When multiple DHCP servers run on the same LAN, devices may receive conflicting settings and either lose connectivity or bypass the intended gateway. Loon can detect other DHCP servers and notify you. It can also stop Loon DHCP automatically when another server is discovered.

Enable DHCP with the setup wizard​

  1. Open Gateway in the Loon4Mac sidebar and select DHCP.
  2. Turn on Enable DHCP to open the initial setup wizard.
  3. Select the Ethernet interface connected to the LAN.
  4. Confirm that the interface uses a static IPv4 address and that no other DHCP server is running on the LAN.
  5. Configure the address pool, subnet mask, router address, and DNS.
  6. Enable Start with VPN if needed, then complete the setup.

After DHCP starts successfully, turn the device's Wi-Fi off and on or reconnect its Ethernet cable. The device requests new network settings and appears in Loon's online device list. Devices using Loon DHCP display a DHCP badge.

Configuration options​

OptionPurpose
Start and end addressesThe IPv4 address range Loon can assign. It must be in the current LAN subnet and exclude addresses used by the router, the Mac, and the Loon gateway.
Subnet maskDefines the IPv4 subnet and should match the current LAN configuration.
Router addressThe default gateway used when a device does not use the Loon gateway. This is normally the LAN router's address.
DNS serverThe DNS address assigned to devices. When Loon UDP DNS interception is disabled, devices query this address directly.
Lease durationHow long a device may use its current address. Devices normally renew before the lease expires.
Use Loon as the default gatewayRoutes device traffic through Loon. The Loon gateway must remain enabled.
Intercept UDP DNSLets Loon intercept the device's UDP DNS traffic. The Loon gateway must remain enabled.
Stop when another DHCP server is foundStops Loon DHCP and sends a notification when another DHCP server is detected.
Start with VPNStarts DHCP with the current configuration whenever Loon VPN starts.

After these options change, new devices and devices renewing their leases receive the current configuration. Loon tries to preserve existing addresses, but an address that is not reserved may still be assigned to another device when necessary.

Use DHCP with the Loon gateway​

DHCP and the gateway are independent features and can be enabled separately:

  • With DHCP only, Loon can assign addresses while devices continue using the LAN router as their default gateway.
  • With DHCP and the gateway enabled, all devices or selected devices can be routed through Loon.
  • Use Loon as the default gateway and Intercept UDP DNS affect future DHCP responses. They do not immediately replace settings in an active lease, so the device must reconnect or renew its lease.

If a device is set to Use Loon Gateway while its UDP DNS policy still follows the DHCP default, Loon also enables UDP DNS interception and assigns Loon DNS to that device. This allows domain-based rules to work correctly.

Manage individual devices​

Right-click a device in the device list to configure:

  • Gateway policy: Follow the DHCP default, use the Loon gateway, or use the LAN gateway.
  • UDP DNS policy: Follow the DHCP default, let Loon intercept it, or do not intercept it.
  • IP management: Use an automatic IP or reserve a fixed address within the pool.

Policies are stored by MAC address and remain in effect the next time the device joins. After changing a policy, reconnect the device or wait for it to renew its DHCP lease.

The DHCP page also provides a read-only lease list and address reservation management. Loon prefers to renew a device with its existing address. Once an address is reserved, it is no longer assigned to other devices.

DHCP and IPv6​

Loon DHCP currently provides DHCPv4. The address pool, subnet mask, router address, and reserved IP settings apply only to IPv4. Loon does not provide DHCPv6, but connected devices can still use IPv6.

IPv6 configuration is delivered through IPv6 RA (Router Advertisement) rather than DHCPv6:

  • Device uses the LAN gateway: Loon DHCP can provide the IPv4 configuration, while the existing router continues to provide the IPv6 address, route, and DNS.
  • Device uses the Loon gateway: After detecting a usable /64 prefix, the Loon IPv6 gateway sends IPv6 RA to that device with an IPv6 route and Loon IPv6 DNS at fd27:712::3.
  • Loon DHCP is enabled without the Loon gateway: The device can still obtain IPv6 configuration from the existing router, but its IPv6 traffic is not handled by the Loon gateway.

After changing a device's gateway or UDP DNS policy, reconnect it to the network. DHCP renewal updates its IPv4 configuration, while a new IPv6 RA updates its IPv6 route and DNS.

If the upstream network does not provide a usable IPv6 /64 prefix, devices can still use the IPv4 settings assigned by Loon. The absence of IPv6 does not stop DHCPv4.

What happens when DHCP is disabled?​

  • Devices with manually configured static IP addresses are not directly affected.
  • Devices with active leases normally continue using their existing settings until the leases expire.
  • If no other DHCP server is available, devices cannot obtain new settings when they reconnect or renew their leases.
  • Before restoring the router's DHCP service, confirm that its address pool does not conflict with Loon's reserved addresses or addresses currently in use, then reconnect the devices.

Technical overview​

Loon DHCP runs inside Loon's macOS network extension. It receives DHCP requests through the selected Ethernet interface and responds with the IP address, gateway, DNS server, and lease duration.

Leases and device policies are stored in a separate database, allowing Loon to recognize existing devices after a restart and preserve their previous addresses when possible. New devices and renewing devices receive responses based on the current DHCP configuration.

The DHCP service assigns IPv4 addresses and does not provide DHCPv6. IPv6 uses a separate RA flow and does not affect Loon DHCP's management of IPv4 leases.

FAQ​

A device still receives an address from the router​

Another DHCP server is probably still running on the LAN. Disable DHCP on the router or other device, then reconnect the client. You can also check Loon's DHCP notifications and running status.

A device did not change after the configuration was updated​

DHCP changes take effect when a device next joins the network or renews its lease. Disconnecting and reconnecting the device normally applies the new configuration immediately.

DHCP is running, but a device cannot access the network​

Check that the address pool and subnet mask belong to the current LAN. If the device uses the LAN gateway, verify the Router Address. If it uses the Loon gateway, check that the Loon gateway is running and that the DNS policy matches the gateway policy.

entry.title: Loon4Mac LAN Gateway Guide
entry.summary: Learn the requirements, setup process, device configuration, DNS options, and supported features of the Loon4Mac gateway.
entry.content:
The gateway feature in Loon4Mac (Build 1007+) lets phones, tablets, computers, and other devices on the same LAN access the network through Loon on your Mac. Client devices do not need Loon installed. Point their default gateway to the address provided by Loon to use Loon's routing rules, policies, and proxy nodes.

When to use it​

  • Temporarily route a phone, TV, game console, or another computer through Loon.
  • Connect a device that cannot run proxy software but supports manual IP, gateway, and DNS settings.
  • View device status, request counts, and traffic centrally on your Mac.
  • Use Loon DHCP to assign gateway and DNS policies to individual devices automatically.

Before you begin​

Check the following requirements before enabling the gateway:

  1. Your Mac is connected through wired Ethernet. The gateway currently uses a wired interface to join the LAN and cannot provide gateway service through Wi-Fi.
  2. Loon VPN is connected. The gateway runs inside Loon's network extension and cannot forward device traffic while the VPN is disconnected.
  3. Your Mac will remain awake. Devices using the Loon gateway lose connectivity if the Mac sleeps, Ethernet disconnects, or the VPN stops.
  4. The gateway IP is not used by another device. Automatic configuration selects an available interface and address. For manual configuration, choose an unused address in the current LAN subnet.
  5. No other virtualization software is using bridged networking. The Loon gateway uses VM bridged networking and cannot run alongside bridged mode in software such as Parallels Desktop or VMware Fusion.

For long-term use, assign a stable IPv4 address to the Mac's Ethernet interface. This is optional when using only the gateway, but a static IPv4 address is required when Loon DHCP is also enabled.

Enable the gateway​

  1. Connect the Mac to the wired LAN and connect Loon VPN.
  2. Open Gateway in the Loon4Mac sidebar and select Gateway Configuration.
  3. Select the Ethernet interface connected to the LAN.
  4. Use automatic configuration or enter an unused gateway IP.
  5. Turn on Start Gateway.

To restore the gateway automatically whenever Loon VPN connects, enable Start with VPN. This option controls startup behavior only; the Start Gateway switch displays and controls the current running state.

If the interface is unavailable, the address is already in use, or the configuration is incomplete, the page displays the reason startup failed. When an interruption is caused by a disconnected cable or temporarily unavailable interface, Loon attempts to restore the gateway after the interface returns and all startup requirements are met.

Connect a device​

There are two ways to connect devices to the Loon gateway.

Manual configuration​

Keep the device on the current subnet and enter the following values in its network settings:

  • IP address: An unused address on the current LAN.
  • Subnet mask: The same mask used by the existing LAN.
  • Router or default gateway: The gateway IP displayed on the Loon gateway page.
  • DNS: Choose an option from the DNS section below.

Loon DHCP​

When Loon DHCP is enabled, it can assign the IP address, gateway, and DNS automatically. DHCP supports global defaults and per-device settings for the Loon gateway, UDP DNS interception, and reserved IP addresses. See the Loon4Mac DHCP Guide for detailed instructions.

Choosing a DNS setting​

The DNS setting determines whether domain requests can fully use Loon's routing rules and Fake-IP features.

DNS settingPath and use case
198.19.0.3Uses Loon's Fake-IP DNS and is suitable for devices that need domain-based routing rules.
Router DNS, such as 192.168.2.1DNS is normally handled by the router. Without UDP DNS interception, Loon may not receive complete domain information.
Public DNS, such as 223.5.5.5Queries go directly to the public DNS server. Without UDP DNS interception, the device does not use Loon's Fake-IP DNS.

If a device already uses the Loon gateway, enabling Loon UDP DNS interception is recommended. With Loon DHCP, this can be configured globally or as a per-device policy.

Supported features​

  • IPv4 gateway forwarding through Loon rules, policies, and nodes.
  • IPv6 TCP, UDP, and ICMPv6 forwarding, plus Loon IPv6 DNS.
  • Online and offline device lists with names, IP addresses, MAC addresses, and device icons.
  • Per-device request counts, active connections, upload traffic, and download traffic.
  • Device connection history and traffic records.
  • Per-device gateway policies, UDP DNS policies, and reserved IP addresses through Loon DHCP.
  • Notifications for startup failures, service interruptions, and newly connected devices.

Device names and types come from information announced by each device and from LAN discovery. Some devices do not expose a complete name and may appear with a generic name or an unknown-device icon.

IPv6 gateway​

The IPv6 gateway works automatically with the Loon gateway and does not need a separate switch. When the wired network provides a usable IPv6 /64 prefix, devices using the Loon gateway automatically receive IPv6 routing and DNS information. Their IPv6 traffic uses the same Loon rules, policies, and proxy nodes.

Clients normally require no manual IPv6 configuration. Reconnect the device after enabling the gateway. If the current network does not support IPv6, the IPv4 gateway continues to work normally. Loon DHCP handles IPv4 configuration only and does not provide DHCPv6.

Technical overview​

Loon4Mac uses macOS VMNET to attach the selected Ethernet interface to the Loon network extension. IPv4 devices locate the Loon gateway through ARP, while IPv6 devices use Router Advertisements and Neighbor Discovery. Traffic sent to the Loon gateway enters Loon's existing rule and proxy processing flow before the Mac forwards it to the destination network.

Only devices whose default gateway points to Loon use this path. Other devices on the LAN and ordinary local communication between devices are not automatically rerouted when the gateway is enabled.

FAQ​

A device has no network access after enabling the gateway​

Check that Loon VPN is connected, the Mac is still connected through Ethernet, the device's default gateway is set to the Loon gateway IP, and that the address is not used by another device. If IP addresses are reachable but domain names are not, check the device's DNS settings.

Can the gateway use Wi-Fi?​

The current version requires a wired Ethernet interface. The Mac itself can remain connected to Wi-Fi, but Wi-Fi cannot be selected as the LAN-facing interface for the Loon gateway.

What happens when the gateway is disabled?​

Devices using the Loon gateway immediately lose that forwarding path. Set their default gateway back to the LAN router, or let them obtain new settings from another DHCP server, to restore normal LAN connectivity.
